summary: Describes the View-based Access Control Model for SNMP, which controls access to management information. It includes a MIB for managing its configuration. It replaces RFC 2265 and was replaced by RFC 2575.

eli5.summary: It decides who may view or change which parts of a device's information. This is an update of an earlier version, later replaced.

questions: how does snmp access control work
subtitle: How an SNMP device decides who may read, write or receive which parts of its management data.

tldr.problem: An SNMP agent holds a lot of management data, and not every user should be able to see or change all of it.
tldr.mechanism: The View-based Access Control Model maps each requester to a group, then looks up a read, write or notify MIB view for that group, context and security level. The request is allowed only if the object is inside that view. A companion MIB lets the tables be configured remotely.
tldr.outcome: This version replaced RFC 2265 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 2575.

today: RFC 2275 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2575, so use that RFC for the current definition. It had itself replaced RFC 2265.

sections.title: Where Access Control Fits
sections.content:
The SNMP architecture in RFC 2271 splits an SNMP engine into a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem and an Access Control Subsystem. This RFC defines one model for that last piece, the View-based Access Control Model (VACM). The text notes that it is not necessarily the only possible access control model.

Access is checked when a Command Responder handles GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest or SetRequest, and when a Notification Originator sends an InformRequest or SNMPv2-Trap. VACM only supplies the checking service. It is up to each application to call it.

The model also needs stored policy. That lives in the engine's Local Configuration Datastore, and the RFC includes a MIB module so a management station can configure it remotely. An IANA note explains that a clerical error in the snmpModules number assignment is corrected here, which is why this memo obsoletes RFC 2265.
sections.eli5: Some devices keep lots of information. VACM is the doorkeeper that checks every request before anything is shown or changed.

sections.title: Groups, Contexts and MIB Views
sections.content:
A group is a set of zero or more securityModel, securityName pairs that all get the same access rights. A given pair maps to at most one group. VACM assumes the securityName was already authenticated and does no authentication of its own. Rights can differ by securityLevel: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv or authPriv.

A context is a collection of management information that an entity can reach. Access to a context goes through a MIB view, a chosen set of managed object types and optionally specific instances. A view is built from view subtrees, each being all object instances that share an OBJECT IDENTIFIER prefix.

Listing a subtree per table column gets long, so a family of view subtrees pairs a family name (an OID) with a bit-string family mask. A mask bit of 1 means that sub-identifier must match and 0 acts as a wildcard. A short mask is implicitly extended with ones, so a zero-length mask means a single subtree. A family can be included in or excluded from a view.

For each context, security model and security level, a group's rights are three views: a read-view, a write-view and a notify-view.
sections.eli5: People are put into teams, and each team gets a list of allowed shelves for looking, for changing and for sending news. Wildcards let one rule cover many similar shelves.

sections.title: The isAccessAllowed Check
sections.content:
Applications call one abstract service, isAccessAllowed, with the security model, security name, security level, view type (read, write or notify), context name and the OID of the object. It returns accessAllowed or an error indication.

The steps run in order. First the vacmContextTable must know the context, otherwise the result is noSuchContext. Then vacmSecurityToGroupTable maps the model and name to a group, otherwise noGroupName. Then vacmAccessTable must have an entry for the group, context, model and level, otherwise noAccessEntry.

The view type picks the read, write or notify view from that entry. An empty view name or no configured view gives noSuchView. If the object is not in the view the result is notInView. Otherwise access is allowed.
sections.eli5: The doorkeeper asks who you are, which room you want and what you want to do. Then he checks his lists one by one, and if you are on every list he lets you in.

sections.title: The VACM Configuration MIB
sections.content:
The module SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB exposes the policy as tables:

  • vacmContextTable lists local contexts by name. It is read-only, and the empty name is the default context.
  • vacmSecurityToGroupTable maps a security model and security name to a group name.
  • vacmAccessTable is indexed by group name, context prefix, security model and security level and holds the read, write and notify view names. A context match of exact or prefix allows simple wildcarding on the context name.
  • vacmViewTreeFamilyTable defines each view as included and excluded subtree families, each with a mask and a type.

When several view entries match an object, the one whose subtree has the most sub-identifiers decides. The vacmViewSpinLock is an advisory lock that cooperating managers can use so that two of them do not edit views at the same time. Instance-level granularity is optional, and an implementation that lacks it must return an inconsistentName error on such a create.
sections.eli5: The doorkeeper's lists are kept in tables that an administrator can edit from far away. A little lock stops two admins from changing the same list at the same moment.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Conformance
sections.content:
VACM checks access using context, group, security model, security level, the operation and the MIB views. It assumes the calling module has already handled authentication and privacy as the passed security level requires.

Two cautions stand out. When creating or deleting view entries, the order recommended in the table description should be followed, or unwanted access may be granted while the table changes. And grouping ignores security level, so administrators should use the level index in vacmAccessTable to keep noAuthNoPriv access separate from authNoPriv and authPriv.

To conform, an implementation MUST implement the MIB module and SHOULD implement the initial configuration from the appendix.
sections.eli5: Edit the lists in the right order, or for a moment the wrong person might get in. Also keep the rules for strangers separate from the rules for people who proved who they are.

sections.title: Initial Configuration
sections.content:
The appendix says an authoritative engine SHOULD be installed with one of three security configurations: initial-minimum-security-configuration, initial-semi-security-configuration or initial-no-access-configuration. The last has no initial setup at all.

Otherwise there is a default context with the empty name and a group named initial for security model 3 (USM). Unauthenticated noAuthNoPriv requests get read and notify access to a restricted view. Authenticated requests (authNoPriv, and authPriv if privacy is supported) get read, write and notify access to the internet view, which is subtree 1.3.6.1.

In the semi-secure setup the restricted view covers only the system, snmp, snmpEngine, snmpMPDStats and usmStats subtrees. In the minimum-secure setup it is the whole 1.3.6.1 subtree.
sections.eli5: A new device ships with starter rules. Strangers may see only a few safe things, while people who prove who they are may see and change everything in the main area.

items.label: Access granted
items.desc: A MIB view was found and the object is in it.

items.label: Denied
items.desc: A view was found but the object is not in it.

items.label: No view
items.desc: No view is configured for the requested view type.

items.label: Unknown context
items.desc: No vacmContextTable entry for the context name.

items.label: No group
items.desc: No vacmSecurityToGroupTable entry for the model and name.

items.label: No access entry
items.desc: No vacmAccessTable entry for the context, group, model and level.
